title: Weather, heat, ultraviolet and wildlife
audience: Field workers, crew leaders and supervisors working outdoors on garden, lawn, irrigation and landscape jobs across Australia.
learningOutcomes: Plan work around heat, ultraviolet exposure, lightning and wind before a job starts.
Recognise the early signs of heat illness in yourself and co-workers and apply the work-rest and hydration controls.
Decide when to stop work, seek shelter and report, using the business's escalation steps.
Recognise common wildlife hazards on outdoor sites and respond without handling animals or nests.

instruction.heading: Why weather is a work hazard
instruction.body: Outdoor work is exposed to conditions that change during a shift. A cool morning can become a hot afternoon, a light breeze can turn into a gusty front, and a thunderstorm can arrive faster than the forecast suggests. Heat, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, lightning, strong wind and wet ground all change how tools behave and how people think. Heat stress reduces concentration, which increases the risk of cuts, falls and vehicle incidents. Lightning and strong wind can bring down branches, lift tarpaulins and make ladders unstable. Before any job, check the forecast and any official weather warnings for the site, and read the business's weather procedure. Write down the conditions under which you will continue, modify the work, or stop. This is the weather trigger matrix for the job, and it should be agreed with your supervisor before work begins. It is a planning tool, not a guarantee, so it must be reviewed again as the day changes.

instruction.heading: Heat, UV and work-rest planning
instruction.body: Heat illness develops gradually. Early signs include headache, dizziness, unusual tiredness, heavy sweating that stops, cramps, nausea and irritability. Any worker who shows these signs must stop, move into shade or a cool area, drink water if they are alert, and be checked by a supervisor. A person who is confused, vomiting, not sweating, or who collapses needs urgent medical help, and the emergency procedure applies. Plan the heaviest tasks for the cooler parts of the day where possible, and schedule regular rest in shade. Keep drinking water available and encourage small regular drinks rather than large amounts all at once. For UV, use the business's sun-protection controls. Shade, long sleeves, a broad-brimmed hat, sunscreen and sunglasses reduce exposure, and shade-seeking should be built into the work plan rather than left to individuals. Do not rely on a cloudy sky as protection. The approach to heat and UV is to change the work, not to push through it.

instruction.heading: Lightning, wind and wet conditions
instruction.body: When lightning is in the area, stop working outdoors and move to a fully enclosed vehicle or building. Wait for a set period after the last thunder before going back outside, following the business's rule. Do not shelter under isolated trees or in open structures such as gazebos, and keep clear of metal fences and equipment during a storm. Strong wind can throw debris, bring down dead branches and make ladders and elevated platforms unsafe. Stop height work and any task that uses a tall tool when gusts make footing or control uncertain. Wet ground and slippery surfaces increase slip risk around mowers, hoses and irrigation fittings. Adjust your method, not only your footwear. Stop and reassess when conditions change, and record the change and the decision in the job record.

instruction.heading: Wildlife and insects
instruction.body: Garden sites contain animals, insects and nests that can injure people. Snakes, spiders, bees, wasps, ants and some caterpillars and marine animals can cause bites, stings or allergic reactions. Treat every nest, hive, burrow and unexplained animal as a hazard. Do not handle, disturb or attempt to remove an animal, and do not use a pesticide on a wildlife hazard unless the business's licensing and training allow it for that product and task. Many native animals are protected and their disturbance may be regulated, so refer the situation to the supervisor and, where needed, to a competent specialist. Before cutting into dense growth, leaf litter or log piles, look and listen first and move slowly. Keep a clear route to the vehicle and carry the first-aid kit and any allergy medication that the worker is authorised to use. Anyone with a known severe allergy must tell the supervisor before the job starts.

instruction.heading: Escalation and verification
instruction.body: A supervisor should check decisions rather than paperwork. In a practical check, a worker should explain which weather conditions would change the plan, show the shade and water arrangements, identify the nearest shelter, and name the person to inform. Stop work immediately for lightning in the area, for a worker who shows heat illness signs, for a wildlife hazard that cannot be isolated, or for wind that makes the task unsafe. Escalate to the supervisor and record the event. Do not restart until the supervisor confirms the conditions have changed.

procedure: Check the forecast and any official weather warnings for the site before arrival, and record the expected conditions.
Agree the continue, modify and stop conditions with the supervisor, and write them on the job sheet.
Set up shade, drinking water, first-aid supplies and a rest schedule before starting heavy work.
Check each worker for heat illness signs at the start of each break and at the start of the afternoon.
Survey the site for nests, hives, burrows and animals, and mark or avoid them without disturbing them.
Monitor the sky and wind during the job. Stop height and tall-tool work when wind or lightning makes it unsafe.
If lightning is in the area, move everyone into a fully enclosed vehicle or building and wait for the business's set period.
Record weather changes, stoppages, rest breaks, any illness or sting, and the decision and the person informed.

workedExamples.situation: A morning hedge and garden clean-up is planned. By midday the temperature has risen, and a storm front is shown on a weather update for the afternoon.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which controls should the supervisor apply, and when do workers stop?
workedExamples.reasoning: Move the heaviest tasks into the cooler morning window and pause the high-exertion work before the storm. Set a rest schedule in shade with water. When the update shows lightning in the area, stop outdoor work, move everyone into an enclosed vehicle or building and wait for the business's rule before going back. Record the change in the job record and check that the client knows the work has been rescheduled.

workedExamples.situation: A worker clearing leaf litter under a shrub is stung several times and reports a rash and difficulty breathing.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first action, and what happens next?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop work, move the worker away from the area, and call emergency services immediately, since breathing difficulty is a sign of a severe allergic reaction. Do not return to the area or try to remove the nest. Follow the business's emergency procedure, record the incident and inform the supervisor. Any worker known to have a severe allergy should have been identified before the job.

equipmentAndPpe: Drinking water and insulated container, sufficient for the planned shift
Broad-brimmed hat, long sleeves and UV-protective clothing
Sunscreen and sunglasses that suit the work
First-aid kit including allergy response items the worker is authorised to use
Two-way or mobile communication suitable for the site

commonErrors.error: Pushing through heat symptoms because the job is nearly finished.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, shade and hydrate the worker, check their condition, and inform the supervisor. Work resumes only when the supervisor confirms.

commonErrors.error: Sheltering under a lone tree or open structure during a storm.
commonErrors.prevention: Move to a fully enclosed vehicle or building, and remain there for the business's set period after the last thunder.

commonErrors.error: Attempting to remove a nest or handle an animal to clear the work area.
commonErrors.prevention: Mark and avoid the hazard, then refer it to the supervisor and any competent specialist. Do not use a pesticide on wildlife unless the task and product are authorised.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a cloudy sky or a long-sleeve shirt alone as UV protection.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the full set of UV controls and build shade and rest into the work plan.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The model Work Health and Safety framework requires duty holders to manage risks, including risks from the environment, so far as is reasonably practicable. Heat, UV, lightning and wildlife are work-environment risks that must be included in the risk assessment. Confirm the state or territory rules that apply to the site.

In Victoria, using a pesticide to control a wildlife hazard needs the right licence. A business that uses a prescribed agricultural chemical for hire or reward needs a commercial operator licence, unless all of its pesticide use is done by a person licensed as a pest control operator under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008. In Victoria, all native birds, mammals, reptiles and frogs are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, and it is illegal to wilfully disturb, hunt, take, trap or kill wildlife without a permit. Removing a nest that holds eggs or birds, trapping wildlife and shooting wildlife need an Authority to Control Wildlife. This lesson does not grant any of these licences or authorities, so check the business's licence position before any treatment.
Many Australian native animals and their habitats are protected. The Victorian rules are set out in the point above. Refer any protected-species issue to the supervisor and a competent specialist.

Heat and UV controls, including the hours of work, rest intervals and the specific thresholds that trigger a change, are set by the business's procedure and the applicable state or territory rules. Specific thresholds are not stated in this draft.

qualityStandard: A weather plan with continue, modify and stop conditions is agreed before the job starts and is recorded on the job sheet.
Shade, drinking water and first-aid supplies are in place before heavy work begins.
Each stop for heat, lightning or wildlife is recorded with the time, the decision and the person informed.
No worker returns to a stopped task until the supervisor confirms the conditions have changed.
documentationEvidence: Weather check and forecast reference recorded at the start of the job.
Written continue, modify and stop conditions signed by the supervisor.
Record of breaks, hydration, any heat illness signs and the actions taken.
Incident record for any sting, bite, allergy or lightning stoppage, including the escalation contact.
summary: Check weather and agree in advance the conditions under which work continues, changes or stops.
Heat illness and UV exposure are managed by changing the work, not by pushing through.
When lightning is in the area, move into an enclosed vehicle or building and wait for the set period.
Do not handle wildlife or nests. Mark, avoid and refer, and treat severe allergy symptoms as an emergency.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker on a garden clean-up feels dizzy, has a headache and has stopped sweating. What is the correct first action?
options: Stop the worker, move them to shade and cool them, then inform the supervisor and assess whether urgent medical help is needed.
Give the worker a short rest, then return them to the same task and check their water intake at the end of the day
Ask the worker to keep going with more water, since they will recover by the end of the shift and the crew can cover for them

knowledgeChecks.question: Lightning is reported within the area during an outdoor job. What should the crew do?
options: Shelter under the nearest large tree until the rain stops and keep an eye on the sky while you wait there
Stop outdoor work and move into a fully enclosed vehicle or building, waiting for the set period before going back outside.
Continue, because the storm is still some distance away and the crew can finish the whole row first today

knowledgeChecks.question: A wasp nest is found in a shrub that must be cut. What is the correct response?
options: Knock the nest down quickly with a tool before the wasps wake up and then spray the area with water
Spray the nest with any product in the van and then carry on with the shrub while the wasps settle
Mark and avoid the nest, do not disturb it, and refer the hazard to the supervisor and a competent specialist.

officialReferences.covers: Says a person conducting a business or undertaking has a duty to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers while they are at work. Does not say that risks from the work environment, such as heat, UV, lightning or wildlife, must be managed; that point remains UNCONFIRMED. Heat and UV thresholds are not stated on this page. Publisher: Safe Work Australia.

officialReferences.title: Pest control licence conditions (Victorian Department of Health)
officialReferences.pageDate: Last updated on 2 January 2025 (page shows 'Updated 2 January 2025')
officialReferences.covers: Says the Agricultural and Veterinary Chemical (Control of Use) Act 1992 requires any person who carries on a business or offers a service to hold a commercial operator licence (COL) when using a prescribed class of agricultural chemical. An exemption applies where the business ensures that all pesticide use is done by a person licensed under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008, which contains the licensing requirements for pest control operators. Does not limit this to particular pests. Publisher: Victorian Department of Health. The page was last updated on 2 January 2025.
